summary:
What We Built
Rendezvous is a browser-based tool where You enter RA and Dec (decimal or sexagesimal) or an object name, and it retrieves SPHEREx image cutouts for that position from NASA/IPAC IRSA and plays them as a blink sequence or tiny video. It provides the user with a vast array of scientific tools to analyze the image cutouts. 

A rendezvous is two things meeting at the same place and time; SPHEREx keeps that appointment with every patch of sky, and the tool lets anyone keep it too.

The Challenge It Addresses
SPHEREx revisits every patch of sky about every six months and observes it at 102 infrared wavelengths. That archive is a powerful way to find moving objects, such as nearby brown dwarfs, comets and possibly distant Solar System bodies, but its raw spectral images are hard for non-specialists to explore. In a blink, a moving object only shows up when you compare the same patch at different times.

Why It Matters
Planet X and the coldest brown dwarfs are both found by motion and by infrared color. Rendezvous puts both clues in one place, for free, with no installation, so students, citizen scientists and researchers can screen any patch of sky in seconds and get encouraged to make great scientific discoveries using this intuitive tool!
details:
THE PROBLEM WE HAD TO SOLVE FIRST

SPHEREx is a spectrometer so every exposure samples a different wavelength. A normal blink of raw frames therefore makes every star flicker, because its brightness changes with wavelength, and that looks exactly like motion or variability. Rendezvous has to remove that false signal before a real mover can be seen.

HOW IT WORKS

We reproject every frame onto a common sky grid, mask pixels the SPHEREx pipeline flagged, and let users co-add exposures (including per detector, to improve signal to noise) or subtract one epoch from another. A static star cancels out. A mover leaves a bright lobe where it was and a dark lobe where it is now. For example, Barnard's Star moves about 10.4 arcseconds per year, and SPHEREx pixels are 6.15 arcseconds wide, so over six months it shifts by roughly one pixel and the lobes are visible.

Clicking any position generates its spectrum, with photometry and astrometry tools for follow-up. Gaia and CatWISE overlays, flags and contamination masks help rule out false alarms such as cosmic-ray hits and detector artefacts.

The five challenge targets are bundled and work offline. Any other coordinate is fetched live from NASA/IPAC IRSA, so new SPHEREx releases appear without rebuilding anything.

THE SKY ATLAS

Nobody can guess long coordinates, so we built 28 ready-made destinations: nearby stars, fast movers, cold brown dwarfs, variable stars, dust and ice regions, and the ecliptic poles where SPHEREx looks most often. Each shows the exact coordinates, corrected for proper motion to today, because catalogue positions from the year 2000 would put a fast star such as Kapteyn's Star several arcminutes off-centre.

WHAT WE CHOSE TO BE HONEST ABOUT

SPHEREx pixels cannot separate close pairs, and very bright stars saturate. We show those flags and include such cases in the Atlas on purpose, so users learn what the data can and cannot do. Large fields mean larger downloads, so the tool asks before big requests and lets users cancel.

TOOLS AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, Vite and Tailwind CSS, built into one file of about 8.8 MB. The FITS parsing, sky projections and photometry are our own code; no astronomy library was used. Fonts: Barlow, Barlow Condensed, IBM Plex Mono. Data: SPHEREx (NASA/IPAC IRSA), Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, AllWISE, 2MASS, DSS2, SIMBAD and HiPS via CDS. Analysis runs in the browser.

The full method, with equations, is in the README on the GitHub repository which is open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 License: https://github.com/Evenstar1/Rendezvous

SI USE

SI tools like Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini were used to help write and debug parts of the source code and documentation. Our team came up with the core idea of Rendezvous, reviewed and tested the output. Best efforts have been made to correct every single subtle inaccuracy we saw the SI models make. The page background and the observatory illustration are SI-generated and carry a visible label in the GitHub repository. All astronomical data shown are real archive data; none was generated by SI. No NASA branding was used or modified using SI.

Live project: https://rendezvous-x.netlify.app
